Choices.A: Reduce R by 100 hours - least contribution per hour sacrificed - costing $2,600
Choices.B: Reduce P by 100 hours - richest accounts contribute first
Choices.C: Spread the cut evenly across products
Choices.D: Reduce Q by 100 hours - middle-ranked balance

CommonTrapReference: Cutting products pro rata instead of by contribution per constraint hour
ExplanationCorrect: Throughput accounting under a shrinking constraint (TOC) ranks products by contribution margin per constraint hour: P $40, Q $32, R $26. When capacity contracts from 1,000 to 900 hours, the 100-hour cut falls on the lowest-ranked use, R: lost contribution = 100 x $26 = $2,600. Protecting P and Q preserves the most contribution per scarce hour, and the freed R hours had the least alternative value anywhere in the plant. Exam trap: allocating the cut pro rata by product size or by historical habit instead of by contribution per hour of the constrained resource.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B sacrifices the HIGHEST-yield hour first (P at $40/hour), inverting the throughput ranking; scarce hours should be stripped from the least profitable use, and cutting P forgoes $4,000 instead of $2,600.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C spreads 100 lost hours evenly (about 33 hours per product), forgoing roughly $3,260 (33 x $40 + 33 x $32 + 34 x $26), which exceeds the necessary $2,600 because it ignores contribution density per hour.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D cuts the middle-ranked product (Q at $32/hour), forgoing $3,200 versus the $2,600 cost of stripping R; ranking by total contribution or seniority rather than by CM per constraint hour drives the error.
FormulaReference: Lost contribution = Hours sacrificed x CM per constraint hour
Stem: Maintenance cuts Barlow constraint from 1,000 to 900 hours next month. Current allocation: P 400 hours at $40/hour; Q 350 at $32; R 250 at $26. Where should the 100-hour cut land?

Choices.B: Fund M - largest incremental CONTRIBUTION ($180K versus $126K and $135K)

CommonTrapReference: Ranking discretionary spends by revenue instead of contribution
ExplanationCorrect: Relevant costing ranks competing discretionary spends by incremental CONTRIBUTION, not revenue: M delivers $180,000; N's $210,000 revenue carries only a 60% margin, yielding $126,000; P yields $135,000. Funding M maximizes the bottom-line return on the identical $50,000 budget, beating the runner-up (P) by $45,000. Business interpretation: campaigns that inflate top-line sales through low-margin volume can destroy value relative to tighter, higher-margin programs, because contribution - not revenue - covers fixed costs and profit. Exam trap: letting the largest revenue number decide the allocation.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A crowns N on the $210,000 revenue headline, but a 60% margin converts it to only $126,000 of contribution - $54,000 behind M - so the flashier program returns less bottom line for the identical $50,000 budget.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C splits a budget across MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE programs, capping every campaign below its standalone contribution and guaranteeing forfeiture of the $180,000 M would have delivered; diversifying rival options leaks value rather than preserving it.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D treats discretionary as worthless, yet declining all three forfeits up to $180,000 of real contribution against the same $50,000 spend; discretion governs approval rights, not whether incremental contribution exists.
Stem: Marketing holds a $50,000 budget for ONE promotion: Program M projects +$180,000 incremental CONTRIBUTION; Program N projects +$210,000 incremental REVENUE on a 60 percent margin; Program P projects +$135,000 contribution. Which program runs?
Topic: C.165 Promotion allocation by incremental contribution
VerifiedChecks: Independent: M +180K beats N +126K and P +135K

Authorities: Managerial accounting theory - differential and avoidable cost analysis

Choices.A: Shut down - avoids the $85K of avoidable fixed costs
Choices.B: Shut down - a quarter cannot run at an operating loss
Choices.C: OPERATE - losing $25K beats losing $100K once the $40K restart penalty is counted
Choices.D: Operate but ignore the restart cost in future seasons

CommonTrapReference: Omitting restart/recertification costs from shutdown analysis
ExplanationCorrect: Differential (relevant) cost analysis: operating contributes $300K - $240K = $60K of margin, less $85K avoidable fixed = -$25K for the quarter. Shutting down avoids the $85K but surrenders the $60K margin and still incurs $60K unavoidable fixed plus the $40K restart/recertification = -$100K. Operating therefore loses $25K versus $100K, better by $75K. Keep-or-drop theory requires counting ALL future avoidable outlays triggered by the decision, including restart penalties. Exam trap: stopping at 'margin below avoidable fixed, so shut it' and missing the restart cost that widens the shutdown loss.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A banks the $85K avoidable saving but ignores the $60K quarterly margin surrendered ($300K - $240K) and the $40K restart bill, moving the result from a $25K operating loss to a $100K shutdown loss.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B imposes a no-operating-loss taboo; the relevant comparison is between losing $25K open and losing $100K closed, and choosing the smaller loss is correct even though neither configuration shows a profit.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D operates but deletes future restart costs from the ledger; each seasonal cycle generates its own recertification outlay, so excluding a recurring, avoidable, future cost corrupts every subsequent shutdown decision.
FormulaReference: Operate delta = CM - Avoidable fixed; Shutdown delta = -(Unavoidable fixed + Restart cost)
Stem: Harborline evaluates shutting a seasonal line for the quarter: revenue $300,000; variable costs $240,000; avoidable fixed costs if operating $85,000; unavoidable fixed costs $60,000 either way; shutting triggers a $40,000 restart and recertification next season. Operate or shut?
Topic: C.166 Seasonal shutdown with restart penalty
VerifiedChecks: Independent: operate -25 vs shut -100 -> operate by 75K

Authorities: Managerial accounting theory - outsourcing and total cost of ownership

Choices.A: Outsource - saves about $45K over three years
Choices.B: Retain - saves about $45K over three years
Choices.C: Outsource - flat pricing always wins against escalators
Choices.D: RETAIN - three-year totals are $630.5K versus $645K, saving roughly $14.5K despite the escalator

CommonTrapReference: Annualizing the first-year gap and ignoring escalators
ExplanationCorrect: Total cost of ownership compares full-horizon cash flows: retaining costs $200K + $210K + $220.5K = $630.5K (5% escalation applied each year), while outsourcing costs 3 x $215K = $645K flat. Retaining saves roughly $14.5K over the term, so the escalator does NOT overturn in-house economics. Relevant-cost comparison over the decision horizon requires summing every escalated year rather than extrapolating year one. Exam trap: multiplying the first-year gap ($215K - $200K = $15K) by three and reporting a fictional $45K saving.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A flips the sign: the vendor bills $645K against $630.5K in-house, so outsourcing destroys roughly $14.5K of value rather than rescuing anything close to $45K.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B chooses correctly but inflates the prize; tripling the year-one gap ($15K x 3 = $45K) skips the 5% escalator that lifts in-house cost to $630.5K and trims the true saving to about $14.5K.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C substitutes dogma for summation; the escalated in-house stream totals $630.5K and undercuts the flat $645K contract, so a 5% escalator is entirely survivable in this comparison.
FormulaReference: Three-year TCO = Sum of escalated annual costs versus contract total
Stem: Paragon compares three-year totals: the in-house line starts at $200,000 escalating 5 percent annually; a vendor bids a flat $215,000 per year. Which way does the relevant comparison go?
Topic: C.167 Outsourcing TCO with escalation clauses

Choices.A: Choose Y - expected UTILITY 60 beats X's 50 even though X's expected MONETARY value is higher
Choices.B: Choose X - expected monetary value governs

CommonTrapReference: Defaulting to EMV when a utility schedule governs
ExplanationCorrect: Expected utility theory (von Neumann-Morgenstern; Raiffa 1968): EU(X) = 0.5 x 100 + 0.5 x 0 = 50; EU(Y) = U(+$20K) = 60. Although X's EMV of $30K exceeds Y's $20K, the decision maker's utility curve penalizes the volatile pair (+$100K/-$40K) enough that the certain $20K ranks higher. Rational choice under stated preferences is Y. Business interpretation: utility calibration captures how a cash-constrained or risk-averse organization weights downside exposure, which raw EMV hides. Exam trap: reflexively picking the higher EMV whenever monetary payoffs are shown, even when a utility schedule is supplied that overrides it.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B lets expected MONEY decide (X at $30K beating Y at $20K), but the supplied utility curve encodes risk aversion; once utilities are stated, they supersede EMV as the ranking standard.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C claims identical scores although expected utilities split 60 to 50 in Y's favor; indifference would require a linear, risk-neutral utility, which the 100-to-0 spread across gains and losses contradicts.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D declares utility analysis powerless to reorder rankings, yet this very matrix reorders them - X wins on money ($30K vs $20K) while Y wins on utility (60 vs 50) because volatility is penalized.
FormulaReference: EU = Sum of p(i) x U(outcome i)
Stem: Treasurer evaluates Project X (50/50 between +$100K and -$40K) against Project Y (certain +$20K), using utility values U(+100K)=100, U(+20K)=60, U(-40K)=0. Which project does the utility-adjusted analysis select?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: EU X=50; EU Y=60 -> choose Y despite lower EMV

Authorities: Decision theory under uncertainty - minimax criterion (Luce and Raiffa)

Choices.A: S1 - its average cost of about $41.7K is lowest
Choices.B: S2 - minimax cost caps the worst outcome at $50K, lower than S1's $60K and S3's $70K
Choices.C: S3 - its best-case cost of $20K is lowest
Choices.D: S2 - because its cross-state total is uniquely lowest

CommonTrapReference: Substituting average or total cost for the worst-case criterion
ExplanationCorrect: Minimax-cost reasoning under uncertainty (Luce and Raiffa, Games and Decisions): for each strategy take the MAXIMUM cost across states - S1: 60, S2: 50, S3: 70 - then select the strategy whose worst case is smallest. S2 caps exposure at $50K and is chosen. Note the built-in distractor trap: S1 and S2 tie on total cost (40+25+60 = 125 versus 50+30+45 = 125), but totals play no role in this criterion; minimax is defensive, protecting against the single worst state. Exam trap: quietly swapping in average, total, or best-case figures when the named criterion is minimax.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A optimizes the average (S1 at about $41.7K per state), a Laplace-style substitution; minimax consults only the worst cell, where S1 reaches $60K and loses to S2's $50K ceiling.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C salutes the best cell in the matrix (S3's $20K), an optimistic-criterion error; under minimax S3's worst case of $70K makes it the most exposed strategy on the board.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D rests on a false premise: cross-state totals TIE (S1 = 125 and S2 = 125), and totals are irrelevant anyway because the criterion caps the single worst state, which S2 does at $50K.
FormulaReference: Minimax cost = minimum over strategies of the maximum cost across states
Stem: Cost matrix (costs, minimize) across three equally possible regulatory states: S1 40/25/60; S2 50/30/45; S3 55/20/70 ($000). Which strategy does minimax COST select?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: max costs 60/50/70 -> S2 caps worst at 50

Authorities: Managerial accounting theory - capital recovery and payback

Choices.C: 6.0 years - cumulative contribution of $400K per year repays the $2.4M development spend in six years

CommonTrapReference: Dividing by unit price instead of unit contribution
ExplanationCorrect: Break-even time extends payback logic to contribution flows: annual contribution = 50,000 units x $8 = $400,000; BET = $2,400,000 / $400,000 = 6.0 years. Only contribution margin - not revenue - retires the development investment, so the launch reaches cash breakeven in year six at plan volume. Capital-recovery analysis treats the outlay as recovered when cumulative contribution equals cumulative spend, after which each incremental unit adds profit. Exam trap: dividing by unit price or volume-adjusted revenue rather than unit contribution, which flatters the recovery clock by ignoring variable costs.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A divides $2.4M by $500K, crediting each unit at $10 (a price-like figure) instead of the $8 contribution; revenue-style numerators flatter the clock because variable costs must still be paid before anything services development.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B halves the true payback by assuming $800K of annual contribution (double the stated volume or a $16 margin); at 50,000 units and $8 contribution, recovery runs $400K per year, not $800K.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D doubles the clock by running only $200K per year through the recovery account, as if half the units converted or variable cost were subtracted twice; plan volume and margin deliver $400K annually.
Stem: Apex spent $2.4M developing its thermostat; each unit contributes $8 and volume is projected at 50,000 per year. What is the break-even TIME on the development spend?
Topic: C.170 Break-even time on development spend
